the role of self-compassion as a coping strategy for dealing with failure.
the role of self-compassion in coping with academic failure.
the effects of academic failure on students’ emotional well-being.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
self-compassion is a positive predictor of achievement goal orientation and adaptive coping, whereas self-compassion has a negative relation to maladaptive coping and shame.
selfcompassion is associated with adaptive achievement goals, which in turn is associated with more adaptive responses when faced with academic failure.
self-compassion and achievement goal theory are both relevant and useful constructs for understanding and explaining students’ academic failure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
self-compassion is an adaptive response to failure, whereas shame is a maladaptive response to failure.
the more self-compassionate students were, the more likely they were to have a growth orientation, to have more self-efficacy, and to have a positive attitude toward learning.
self-compassion is a protective factor against negative affect in the face of failure, but that this protection does not come at the cost of reduced performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the achievement goal approach is a powerful way to understand how students respond when they experience failure.
students who are more self-compassionate tend to have more adaptive goals, and these goals in turn lead them to be more resilient and to cope better with academic failure.
students’ goals are important to consider in the development and implementation of programs to help students cope with academic failure.
